newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs end Tokyo down after failing to hit new highs.
newsitem.headline: JGBs end Tokyo down after failing to hit new highs.

text.p: Key March 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) futures closed lower on Monday after failing to hit new highs in the morning.
The March rose as high as 126.80 in early trade following the yen's rise after the weekend Group of Seven (G7) meeting.

However, the benchmark contract reversed its bullish tone as dealers liquidated long positions after it failed to set record highs. A healthy rise in the Tokyo stock market was also a negative factor, traders said.
The contract ended at 126.33, down 0.23 from Friday's finish. Turnover was 42,686.
The all-time high for any benchmark JGB futures contract is 126.83 set on January 27.

"The yen's rise first boosted JGBs. But the topside was heavier than many had expected. So those who had bought in early trade started to sell to cut losses," said a dealer at a city bank's securities unit.
The dollar was stalled just under 123 yen in late Tokyo trade, compared with around 124.20 yen in Tokyo on Friday.
The G7 nations agreed on Saturday that "major misalignments in exchange markets, noted in our April 1995 communique, have been corrected."

Scattered cash buying was detected from investors in the morning, but their buying was almost nil in the afternoon, traders said. The yield on key cash 182nd 10-year JGBs stood at 2.390 percent at 0717 GMT, up 0.015 from Friday.

"Trade was widely led by day-traders as is often seen on Mondays. Investors were away also because it is a holiday on Tuesday here," the dealer said. The Tokyo financial markets are closed for a national hoilday on Tuesday.
Some traders attributed late weakness in JGBs to comments on Japan's economy from Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau.
Sakakibara said although market participants currently hold the view that market interest rates will continue to move at low levels, it is hard to predict what will happen in the future.
Some traders said the comments implied that it is possible that interest rates may rise in the near future, contrary to the market's current expectations.
But others said they ignored the comments as Japan's private machinery order data released this afternoon was as weak as expected.

Japan's private-sector machinery orders fell 12.8 percent in December from the previous month, the Economic Planning Agency (EPA) said. The EPA also said it expected private machinery orders to fall 8.5 percent in the January-March quarter from the previous quarter.

Japanese interest rates should stay low for the time being as they reflect low demand in the January-March period and after April 1 when the government's public spending is to be reduced, said a dealer at a trust bank dealer. -- Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-3432-8570
